members.name: persuasion_v14
members.instructions: This is a charity-donation chat in which a persuader tries to convince the persuadee to donate part of their task payment to Save the Children. Using the annotation scheme of persuasion strategies and dialogue acts, which category best describes the persuader message to tag (the last message)? Use the earlier chat only as context.

criteria.greeting: Says hello or opens the chat with pleasantries: 'Hi!', 'Hello there', 'How are you today?', 'I'm good, how are you?', including replies to 'how are you?' such as 'I am doing well thank you'.
criteria.thank: Thanks the partner: 'Thank you', 'Thanks so much for your kindness', including thanks combined with a goodbye.
criteria.praise-user: Compliments the persuadee personally: 'You are so generous', 'That's awesome and generous!', 'People like you make the world better.' Also complimenting the persuadee's charitable habits or character, e.g. 'very very good' after they say they donate every six months. Also enthusiastic praise when the persuadee commits to a generous donation ('That's wonderful!' after the persuadee agrees to a $500 donation). A brief 'Awesome.' reacting to the persuadee agreeing to a modest donation is acknowledgement, not praise. Not statements about the donation's effect ('Your donation will be very meaningful to needy children' is logical-appeal), nor reports of the organization's results.
criteria.acknowledgement: Short reaction acknowledging what the partner just said, agreeing or showing understanding: 'I see', 'You are right', 'ok, I understand that', 'Me too', 'Indeed', 'Absolutely', 'Yes they do.' (a bare affirmation, not answering a question), 'Awesome.' after the persuadee says 'Sure I will donate 30%', empathizing with the persuadee's situation ('I understand financial strain I my self have been struggling'). Only for reacting to a statement; replying to a question the persuadee asked is not acknowledgement.
criteria.ask-donation-amount: Asks HOW MUCH the persuadee will donate: 'How much would you like to give?', 'What amount would you feel comfortable donating?'
criteria.proposition-of-donation: Directly asks or proposes that the persuadee donate (without asking the amount): 'Would you be willing to donate some of your payment?', 'Donate some money maybe?', 'Would you consider donating?', suggesting a specific donation ('so we usually suggest a monthly donation of $5').
criteria.foot-in-the-door: Asks for or urges a small first contribution, to get the persuadee to commit a little: 'could you afford maybe fifteen cents?', 'We can all do something - donate a little bit or volunteer to try to help', and any message whose point is simply that even a small amount helps or makes a difference ('Every little bit helps!', 'Something as small as .05 could help.', 'a couple of cents or a couple of dollars might not make a difference in your life but it can make a huge impact on some child's life', 'Even a small donation makes a difference', 'Any donation will help', 'Even if it's small'). But a message that adds reasoning about how small amounts work: adding up across many donors, a concrete outcome they buy, or why they are affordable ('Even small donations, added together, can make a tremendous difference', 'I don't know about you, but I could find $1 in change just lying around the house', the good feeling the donor gets from donating ('Meanwhile, you could feel great about helping those kids who really need your support!'), '$1 can feed a child for a day', 'I could find $1 in change lying around the house') is logical-appeal.
criteria.self-modeling: Persuader states their own intention or habit of donating, as an example to follow: 'I will donate $1 of my payment', 'I usually give to this cause yearly', 'I'll match your donation', including answering 'have you donated?' with 'I have in the past.'
criteria.personal-story: Tells a narrative or personal experience (own or someone else's story) as an example: 'I worked in Africa and saw the difference a few dollars make', a story about a specific child or family.
criteria.emotion-appeal: Tries to evoke emotions such as sadness, guilt, empathy, hope or anger about the children: 'It breaks my heart', 'Imagine if it were your child', 'The suffering children face is terrible', 'They will greatly appreciate it', moving facts stated about children killed, dying, starving or saved ('In the first two months of 2018 alone, 1,000 children were reportedly killed or injured', 'We have not received much support for these children', 'I read an article that said 1000 children were saved from hunger shelters just by donations from online workers'). Also the persuader sharing their own sorrow or helplessness about victims ('Every day I watch the news and hear about victims all over the world and feel kind of powerless'). If the fact is posed as a question to the persuadee ('Did you know...?', 'Are you aware...?'), it is task-related-inquiry.
criteria.logical-appeal: Uses reasoning or evidence about why donating helps: 'Your donation will help many children', 'Your donation will be very meaningful to needy children', 'They can only help when people donate', 'Donations make a huge difference', countering the persuadee's objections with reasons ('we can work all day to make up the small amount we will contribute'), arguing the donation is affordable ('think about the little things you buy, and instead of buying that bag of chips or cup of coffee, donate it to the children'), 'Even small donations, added together, can make a tremendous difference', 'I don't know about you, but I could find $1 in change just lying around the house', the good feeling the donor gets from donating ('Meanwhile, you could feel great about helping those kids who really need your support!'), 'I have donated to them, that is why I can confidently say your money will be put to good use'.
criteria.credibility-appeal: Establishes the credibility or trustworthiness of Save the Children by citing its credentials, reputation, reach, history, or what the organization does and has achieved: 'It's one of the top rated charities', 'They have a presence on every continent', 'It is an international NGO that promotes children's rights', 'it is a trustable fund', 'I really believe in this organization and think it's worthwhile.', 'Our organization gives shelter to those kids', listing what it works on ('Education, poverty issues, healthcare, emergency response.'), defending its impact against the persuadee's doubts ('Just because it is not happening somewhere that you see everyday does not mean that it does not exist.'). Also citing the organization's fundraising results or impact even when it thanks or compliments donors ('This year we are on track to hit 3 million thanks to generous people like you!').
criteria.donation-information: Gives procedural information about how the donation in this task works: deducted from the task payment, the amount can range from $0 to $2, the research team will send it to the charity, the website URL, other ways to contribute such as volunteering ('There are areas that you can volunteer too, if you have the skillset'). But 'We can all do something - donate a little bit or volunteer' stresses that a little helps: foot-in-the-door.
criteria.source-related-inquiry: Asks whether the persuadee knows about the organization: 'Have you heard of Save the Children?', 'Are you familiar with the organization?', 'What do you know about Save the Children?'
criteria.task-related-inquiry: Asks the persuadee's opinion, interest, or expectations about donating or the cause: 'Is this something you care about?', 'Are you interested?', 'Do you think you would help Syrian children if you could?', 'Is there any information I could provide?', 'Can you elaborate?', rhetorical questions inviting the persuadee to consider the cause ('What if i told you that you have the opportunity of a lifetime to make a change in the world?'), challenging questions about the persuadee's view of charities ('and those local charities they give you their financial info?'). Includes 'Did you know...?' / 'Are you aware...?' questions about the problem the children face, e.g. 'Did you know 5.6 million children die every year due to preventable causes?'.
criteria.personal-related-inquiry: Asks about the persuadee's personal life or past experiences relevant to charity: 'Do you donate to charities?', 'Have you ever thought about volunteering for something like this?', 'Do you have children?', 'Where are you from?'. Includes persuasive or rhetorical questions about the persuadee's own habits or spending: 'How much money do you spend on candies that could be helping children in need?'. Must be a question; statements are not inquiries.
criteria.off-task: Unrelated to the donation or the conversation's purpose: remarks about the HIT/survey mechanics, typo corrections. Friendly chit-chat that continues a side topic of the conversation is other.
criteria.other-closing: Closing remarks and goodbyes without thanks: 'Have a great night!', 'I hope you enjoy the rest of your day.'
criteria.other-answer: A bare yes/no or short factual reply to a question the persuadee asked, with no persuasive content (if the answer argues for donating, choose that strategy; replies to 'how are you?' are greeting), e.g. 'Yes, I have heard that.' in reply to 'have you heard that some charities steal money?', 'Her name is Eglantyne Jebb', 'I'm so glad you asked!' (when the persuadee asks how to help), 'Yes, they are', 'I'm not sure of the exact details', confirming the donation amount the persuadee stated.
criteria.other-confirm: Confirms or double-checks the amount the persuadee has decided to donate: 'Alright, just to be sure you want to donate 1 dollar?', 'Half of 1 dollar?' after the persuadee says 'Let's do half - $1'.
criteria.other-why-not: Asks why the persuadee does not want to donate or what is stopping them: 'why do you don't want to donate?'
criteria.other-misc: Any other message that fits none of the options above, e.g. vague comments like 'It is a great choice.', 'Just think.', 'You get to feel good about yourself and do a good thing at the same time.' (about volunteering, not the donation), 'How do you know that nothing in your neighborhood is funded by them?' (a sarcastic question arguing back at the persuadee), 'John Cena is amazing.' (chit-chat after the persuadee mentions celebrities supporting causes), 'wish that we could, but like all working on MTurk we are poor ourselves' (in reply to 'should we give more?').
